extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, researchers, and research-integrity professionals (readers of Retraction Watch)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reporting about identifying and responding to peer-review manipulation (fake/illegitimate reviewer accounts, paper-mill submissions) and appropriate publisher/editor actions (investigation, contacting affected parties, and retraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid acceptance based on one illegitimate reviewer report
rubrics_metrics.description: “the acceptance of this article was partly based upon the positive advice of one illegitimate reviewer report.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An article should not be accepted on the basis of a single reviewer report if that report's provenance is questionable. The example notice shows that acceptance tied to a single illegitimate report merits investigation and can lead to retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify reviewer identity; do not treat suggested reviewers as automatically independent
rubrics_metrics.description: “The report was submitted from an email account which was provided to the journal as a suggested reviewer during the submission of the article. Although purportedly a real reviewer account, the Editors have concluded that this was not of an appropriate, independent reviewer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals must verify that suggested reviewer accounts are genuine and independent (email/account provenance, affiliation, prior publications) before relying on their recommendations. The publisher investigated and found many suggested reviewer accounts to be illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review manipulation is a violation of publishing ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: “This manipulation of the peer-review process represents a clear violation of the fundamentals of peer review, our publishing policies, and publishing ethics standards.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulating peer review (fake reviewers, assumed identities) breaches core ethical standards and justifies corrective actions such as apology, correction, or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers should investigate whistleblower reports and patterns across submissions/issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Anna Abalkina noted patterns of suspect papers; the publisher alerted editors-in-chief and the ethics team and investigated provided reviewer-account lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When external whistleblowers or pattern detectors flag multiple suspect papers (same issue, same journal, similar writing), publishers should run a coordinated investigation rather than treating items in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction is appropriate when peer-review manipulation is confirmed
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Editors decided the retraction of 47 papers (in May 2022).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirmed manipulation of the peer-review process (e.g., use of illegitimate reviewer accounts that influenced acceptance) supports retraction of affected articles as a remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request and consider corresponding authors' responses before final action
rubrics_metrics.description: “The corresponding authors were requested to comment on the allegations and eventually the Editors decided the retraction of 47 papers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should solicit explanations from corresponding authors as part of due process before making final decisions such as retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact genuine individuals whose identities may have been misused
rubrics_metrics.description: “During the investigation genuine persons whose names were apparently used to create the illegitimate reviewer accounts were contacted…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should seek to notify and verify with legitimate reviewers whose names were allegedly co-opted, both to confirm misuse and to protect reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and review lists of suspect reviewer accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: “the publisher provided ethics with the list of suspect reviewer accounts. The ethics team confirmed then the suspicions on the initially provided reviewer accounts and we also found new illegitimate reviewer accounts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping and iteratively reviewing compiled lists of suspect accounts helps identify networks of illegitimate reviewers and supports broader investigative efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use software and systematic checks to detect paper mills and plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters noted: “There is the software available to do that, as there is for checking potential plagiarism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and editors should deploy dedicated tools and routine screening to detect likely paper-mill products, plagiarism, and other textual/pattern indicators rather than relying solely on manual inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors should proactively inspect submissions and desk-reject out-of-scope/low-quality work
rubrics_metrics.description: A former editor: “I always inspected submissions ... and desk-rejected about half of them (on grounds of scope and quality). And we would hardly ever accept reviewers on the suggestion of an author, unless we were running out of options.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active editorial triage (desk rejection for scope/quality) reduces reliance on external review and lowers the chance that manipulated reviews lead to inappropriate acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure adequate resourcing and fair compensation for editorial staff to enable proper vetting
rubrics_metrics.description: A commenter: vetting took hours a day while being paid a tiny stipend; under-resourcing meant abuse and inadequate response from publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should provide sufficient staff time, training, and compensation so editors/managers can perform necessary vetting and ethical oversight; otherwise quality control suffers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be suspicious of authors with an unusually high publication rate in short timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am very suspicious of someone who has too many publications in a short period of time outside of the turnaround time frame to publishing. … That is what they want—people will always find a way to game the system.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anomalous publication patterns (many rapid publications) can be a red flag for gaming the system or paper-mill involvement and merit closer scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider financial incentives (e.g., open-access charges) as a risk factor for lapses in rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment: “It would be worthwhile finding out if this journal had a certain dependence on Open Access submissions and hence paper charges, which tends to encourage a less rigorous peer review process.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether journal business models or article charges create pressures that may reduce review rigor; financial incentives can correlate with higher risk of compromised review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers should promptly acknowledge and respond to external reports of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Abalkina noted she did not receive a response when she pointed out the suspect articles to Elsevier; later the publisher acted after her public tweet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely and transparent responses to external notifications (including whistleblowers and public reports) improve detection and trust; ignoring such reports allows problems to persist.
